lessons.title: One league, one table
lessons.objective: You can explain how the league table decides the champion.

payload.prompt: A team wins two matches, draws one and loses one. How many points?

options.text: 5 points
6 points
7 points

explanation.correct: Right. Two wins are 6 points, the draw adds 1, and the loss adds nothing, so 7 in total.
explanation.incorrect: Three points per win and one per draw: 2 x 3 = 6, plus 1 for the draw, plus 0 for the loss makes 7.
explanation.sayThisLine: Two wins and a draw, that's seven points from four games.

payload.prompt: Same points: Arsenal's goal difference is +32, City's +38. Who is ahead?

options.text: Arsenal, because they are alphabetically first
City, on the better goal difference
Arsenal, because they played more home games

explanation.correct: Right. In the Premier League, goal difference (goals scored minus goals conceded) is the first tiebreaker when points are level, then goals scored.
explanation.incorrect: Level on points, the Premier League looks at goal difference first. City's +38 beats +32, so they sit higher. Goals scored is the next tiebreaker.
explanation.sayThisLine: We're level on points, but their goal difference is better.

payload.prompt: Complete how a league season works.
payload.template: In a 20-team league where everyone plays everyone home and away, each team plays {{games}} matches, and the champion is the team with the most {{measure}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Each team plays the other 19 twice, so 38 matches, and the table is decided by points.
explanation.incorrect: Nineteen opponents, home and away, gives 38 matches. The league table ranks teams by points, not by wins or goals alone.

payload.prompt: Team X has more wins, but Team Y has more points. Does Y win the league?

scene.alt: Team X won 24 matches and drew 4. Team Y won 22 matches and drew 12.

explanation.correct: Yes. The league is decided by points, not wins. Team Y has 78 points and Team X has 76.
explanation.incorrect: Draws count for a point each, so a team with fewer wins can still top the table. Team Y has 78 points to Team X's 76.
explanation.sayThisLine: More points beats more wins, every time.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: We can't afford draws now, it's basically a loss for us.

options.text: She is chasing something where dropped points really matter
A draw only gives one point when she needs three
Draws are worth three points
Her team has been relegated

payload.translation: Her team is in a tight title or promotion race, where one point from a draw feels like two dropped points compared with a win.

followUps.why: Shows you grasp what is at stake.

followUps.line: So it's three points or nothing from here?
followUps.why: A light, curious way to show you follow the maths.

lessons.title: Going up and going down
lessons.objective: You can explain promotion and relegation.

payload.prompt: Match the ladder term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A club near the top of the lower division moves up a level
A club near the bottom of a division drops down a level
Finishing high enough above the drop zone to remain in the division
The levels of leagues linked by promotion and relegation

explanation.summary: Promotion and relegation link the leagues into a ladder. Every season some clubs go up, some go down and some survive by a point.
explanation.sayThisLine: Three up, three down, and it all comes down to the last day.

payload.prompt: Where do the promoted teams come from?

options.text: The top of the league below
A draft
The previous season's runners-up

explanation.correct: Right. The top teams from the division below get promoted up. It's a ladder system.
explanation.incorrect: Promotion comes from the division below. The best teams down there go up; the worst teams here go down.

payload.prompt: Complete the Premier League ladder.
payload.template: In the Premier League, {{down}} clubs are relegated each season, and {{up}} clubs are promoted from the Championship.

explanation.correct: Right. The bottom three go down and three come up from the Championship: two automatic places and one playoff winner.
explanation.incorrect: Three clubs go down and three come up: the top two in the Championship, plus the winner of the promotion playoff.

statement.speaker: Her
statement.text: Three go down and it gets brutal at the bottom.

options.text: Three clubs are relegated at the end of the season
The bottom of the table is a tense fight to stay up
Three players are leaving the club
Three managers have been sacked

payload.translation: In the Premier League the bottom three clubs drop into the Championship, so teams near the bottom are fighting to stay up, and it gets very tense.

followUps.line: How many points do they need to stay up?
followUps.why: Turns her comment into a real football question.

followUps.line: Who's most in trouble right now?
followUps.why: Invites her to tell you more.

payload.prompt: MLS has promotion and relegation like the Premier League. True or false?

scene.alt: A table of MLS clubs at the end of the season with no clubs dropping to a lower division.

explanation.correct: False. MLS has no relegation: clubs stay in the league whatever their position, and the season ends with the playoffs and the MLS Cup.
explanation.incorrect: MLS is a closed league. Bottom clubs stay put, although the Supporters' Shield goes to the team with the most points.
explanation.sayThisLine: No relegation in MLS, so no drop to fear.

lessons.title: Domestic cups
lessons.objective: You can explain why the cup produces upsets.

payload.prompt: What is a domestic cup?

options.text: A knockout tournament inside one country where small clubs face giants
A league for smaller teams
A trophy for the best defensive team

explanation.correct: Right. The cup (like the FA Cup or Copa del Rey) is a knockout, so any team can beat any other team in one match.
explanation.incorrect: A domestic cup is a knockout tournament inside one country. Small clubs face giants, and that's where upsets happen.

payload.prompt: Why do small teams have a chance to beat big teams in the cup?

options.text: Because it's one match, not a season-long series
Because big teams don't play their best players
Because small teams get extra players

explanation.correct: Right. A single match is a lottery; anyone can win one night. In the league, form and strength over 38 games decide it.
explanation.incorrect: It's the knockout format. One match means anything can happen. The best league finisher might not win the cup.

payload.prompt: Complete how a domestic cup works.
payload.template: A domestic cup is a {{format}} competition, and clubs from across the {{pyramid}} can take part.

explanation.correct: Right. It is a knockout, so one loss ends your run, and many cups welcome clubs from several divisions.
explanation.incorrect: Cups like the FA Cup are knockout competitions. Lose once and you are out, which is why small clubs from lower divisions can dream of beating giants.

statement.speaker: Him
statement.text: It's the cup, so anything can happen.

options.text: A single knockout match can produce an upset
Small clubs sometimes beat giants in cup ties
Cup games are played over a full season
The referee is picking a winner

payload.translation: In a knockout cup, one match decides a tie, so a smaller side can beat a much stronger opponent on the day.

followUps.line: Which giant are you hoping falls this round?
followUps.why: Friendly and shows you know upsets happen.

followUps.line: Remember when a lower-league team knocked out a top side?

payload.prompt: Match the cup term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: A result almost no one expected, such as a lower-league club beating a top side
A smaller club knocking out a much bigger one
A team winning round after round and going deep into the competition

explanation.summary: Cups are romantic because one bad day can end a giant's season, and a small club can suddenly have a cup run.
explanation.sayThisLine: That was some cup run, from round one to the semi-final.

lessons.title: Europe and qualification
lessons.objective: You can explain how a club qualifies for the Champions League.

payload.prompt: How do clubs get into European competitions like the Champions League?

options.text: They win a domestic cup
They finish high enough in their league
They are invited by UEFA

explanation.correct: Right. League position is the main path. Finishing near the top of the table, often top four or five depending on how many places the country earns that year, gets you Champions League football.
explanation.incorrect: Clubs mostly qualify through league position. The number of Champions League spots each country receives can change from year to year.
explanation.sayThisLine: We need to finish top four to get Champions League football.

payload.prompt: Match the European competition to its rank.

pairs.definition: The top European club competition; mainly for the best league finishers
The second-tier European competition for mid-table finishers and cup winners
The newest, third-tier European competition

explanation.summary: UEFA runs three tiers: the Champions League at the top, the Europa League next, and the Conference League as the third competition.
explanation.sayThisLine: Champions League is the big one, Europa League is next.

statement.speaker: Him
statement.text: We just need to hang on to top four this season.

options.text: They want to qualify for the Champions League
They are trying to finish in the top places of the league table
There are only four teams in Europe
They are being relegated

payload.translation: His team wants to finish high enough in the league to earn a Champions League place for next season.

followUps.line: How many points is the gap now?
Who else is in that race?
followUps.why: Encourages him to talk about rivals.

payload.prompt: A club wins the FA Cup but finishes tenth. Can it still play in Europe?

scene.alt: A team lifts a domestic cup after a mid-table league finish.

explanation.correct: Yes. The FA Cup winner earns a place in European competition, usually the Europa League, even after a mid-table league finish.
explanation.incorrect: In England the FA Cup winner gets a European place. If that club already qualified another way, the place passes on under the competition's rules.
explanation.sayThisLine: Win the cup and you might play in Europe next year.

payload.prompt: When fans say 'We're fighting for Europe', what do they mean?

options.text: They are trying to finish high enough to qualify for European competitions
They are playing teams from Europe
They are moving to Europe

explanation.correct: Right. Fighting for Europe means trying to finish high enough to qualify for the Champions League, Europa League or Conference League. That brings extra matches, money and prestige.
explanation.incorrect: When fans say a club is fighting for Europe, they mean it is trying to finish high enough in the league table to earn a European place.

lessons.title: Transfers, loans and contracts
lessons.objective: You can explain a loan, a fee and a free transfer.

payload.prompt: Match the transfer term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: The price one club pays another to sign a player under contract
A player joins another club for a set period, usually a season
A player moves for no fee because his contract has run out

explanation.summary: A fee is money paid to a club. A loan is temporary. A free transfer happens when the contract has ended, so the old club gets nothing.
explanation.sayThisLine: He's out of contract in the summer, so it's a free transfer.

payload.prompt: When can clubs sign new players?

options.text: Only during the transfer window, usually summer and January
Anytime during the season
Only before the season starts

explanation.correct: Right. The transfer window is a fixed period. Summer is the big one and January is the smaller one. Free agents without a club can often still sign outside it.
explanation.incorrect: Clubs can generally only register new players in the windows: summer and January. Unattached free agents can often still sign outside them.

payload.prompt: A young player wants more games. What should the club do?

situation.narrative: A 19-year-old has come through the academy, but he is stuck behind two senior players and the manager is not sure he is ready.

options.label: Loan him to a club where he will start
options.consequence: He plays regularly, grows, and comes back stronger. The club keeps the contract.
considerations: Regular football helps young players develop

options.label: Sell him now for a fee
options.consequence: It brings money, but the club gives up a player who might become good.
considerations: But it removes a home-grown asset

options.label: Keep him on the bench
options.consequence: He barely plays, loses confidence and may leave for free later.

payload.expertNote: Clubs often use loans as a development step. The trade-off is that a loaned player is away from the manager's day-to-day coaching, so clubs choose the loan club carefully.
payload.sayThisLine: Send him out on loan so he can play every week.

payload.prompt: A player's contract has run out and he signs for a new club. Does the new club pay a fee?

scene.alt: A footballer signs for a new club after his old contract has expired.

explanation.correct: No. With an expired contract he is a free agent, so the new club does not pay a transfer fee, although it may pay a signing bonus and wages.
explanation.incorrect: Once a contract ends there is nothing left for another club to buy from the old one, so the move is free.
explanation.sayThisLine: His contract's up in the summer, so it's a free transfer.

payload.prompt: He's on loan with an option to buy. What does that mean?

options.text: The borrowing club can decide to buy his contract at a set price
The player can choose to leave anytime
The original club has to sell him

explanation.correct: Right. An option to buy lets the borrowing club decide later whether to make the move permanent, at a price agreed in advance.
explanation.incorrect: An option to buy is a choice for the club that borrowed the player. If he performs well, they can pay the agreed fee and keep him.

lessons.title: Academy and the club machine
lessons.objective: You can explain the roles of manager, academy and sporting director.

payload.prompt: What is a club's academy?

options.text: A youth system that develops young players who might reach the first team
A school for fans
A training facility for retired players

explanation.correct: Right. The academy brings in kids, trains them, and either sells them or promotes them to the first team.
explanation.incorrect: An academy is the youth system. You hear fans say a player 'came through the academy' when he rose from the youth teams.

payload.prompt: Match the club job to who does it.

pairs.definition: Picks the team and decides how the side plays on match day
Runs recruitment and long-term planning across the squad
The youth system that develops young players for the first team
Owns the club and sets the overall budget

explanation.summary: The manager works on the day-to-day football, the sporting director plans the squad, the academy grows young talent and the owner backs it all.
explanation.sayThisLine: The manager picks the team, and the sporting director builds the squad.

payload.prompt: Who normally picks the starting eleven each week?

scene.alt: Team news has just been announced ahead of a match.

explanation.correct: The manager picks the team and tactics. The sporting director works on recruitment and the longer-term plan.
explanation.incorrect: Team selection belongs to the manager or head coach. The sporting director is more about transfers, contracts and building the squad.
explanation.sayThisLine: The manager picks the team, and that's that.

statement.speaker: Him
statement.text: The manager wanted him but the sporting director wouldn't pay the fee.

options.text: The manager and the sporting director disagreed about a signing
The club felt the fee was too high for its budget
The player refused to move
The manager owns the club

payload.translation: The manager wanted to sign a player, but the sporting director, who manages recruitment and the transfer budget, felt the price was too high.

followUps.line: Who ends up deciding in the end?
followUps.why: Invites him to explain club roles.

payload.prompt: Fans call a player 'one of our own'. What do they usually mean?

options.text: He came through the club's academy
He signed on a free transfer
He is the cheapest player in the squad

explanation.correct: Right. It usually means an academy graduate who grew up at the club. Fans love that connection, and clubs also have homegrown-player rules in their squad lists.
explanation.incorrect: 'One of our own' points to a player who rose through the club's youth system, not to price or how he arrived.

lessons.title: Derbies and matchday culture
lessons.objective: You can explain why derbies, supporter culture and spending rules matter.

payload.prompt: What is a derby?

options.text: A match between local rivals with deep history
A cup competition
An international tournament

explanation.correct: Right. A derby is more than three points; it's pride, history and local bragging rights.
explanation.incorrect: A derby is a local rivalry match. The form book goes out the window; anything can happen when neighbours play.

payload.prompt: In a derby, the league table always tells you who wins. True or false?

scene.alt: Two local rivals meet, and the team lower in the table is playing at home.

explanation.correct: False. Derbies are famous for ignoring the form book, because pride and emotion lift the underdog.
explanation.incorrect: There is no guarantee in a derby. Fans say to throw the form book out because the weaker team often plays out of its skin.
explanation.sayThisLine: In a derby, throw the form book out.

payload.prompt: Match the fan-culture term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Highly organised fan groups known for chants and choreography
A large choreographed banner or display shown by supporters
A fan-run organisation that gives supporters a voice in how the club is run
The section of the stadium given to the visiting fans

explanation.summary: Supporter culture is more than noise. Groups shape the atmosphere, the displays and sometimes the club's decisions.
explanation.sayThisLine: The tifo before kick-off was incredible.

payload.prompt: Why do leagues have spending rules?

options.text: To prevent rich clubs from dominating too completely
To make everyone equal
To reduce player salaries

explanation.correct: Right. Rules such as the Premier League's squad-cost limit and UEFA's squad cost ratio try to stop clubs from overspending and to keep the competition fairer.
explanation.incorrect: Spending rules exist to keep clubs financially sustainable and to limit how far a rich owner can outspend everyone else.

statement.speaker: Him
statement.text: It's a derby, throw the form book out.

options.text: Form does not matter as much in a derby
The underdog often plays above its level
The league table is not used
The referee will pick the winner

payload.translation: In derbies, emotion and pride can outweigh recent form, so the weaker team has a real chance.

followUps.line: Who do you think steps up in a derby?
followUps.why: Invites him to share his read.

followUps.line: What's the best derby you've ever watched?
followUps.why: Great way to hear a story.

payload.title: Derby day nerves
payload.setting: His team plays its local rival tomorrow, and he is nervous.

exchanges.theirMessage: Tomorrow's the derby. I can barely eat. We're the underdogs but it's the one that matters.

replies.text: Underdogs can be dangerous in derbies, right? Throw the form book out.
replies.theirResponse: Exactly! That's what I keep telling myself.
replies.coachNote: Uses the phrase correctly and shows you follow the idea.

replies.theirResponse: Three points? It's so much more than that.
replies.coachNote: Undersells what a derby means to fans.

replies.text: What's it feel like when your team scores against them?
replies.theirResponse: Nothing beats it. The whole stadium shakes.
replies.coachNote: An open question that invites a story.

exchanges.theirMessage: The fans are planning a big tifo before kick-off. It's going to be huge.

replies.text: I love that. Is the whole end in on it?
replies.theirResponse: Yes! Ultras have been painting it for weeks.
replies.coachNote: Shows interest in the culture behind the game.

replies.theirResponse: A giant banner display, like a mosaic. You'll see it.

payload.closingNote: Derby talk is about emotion and history. Curiosity about what it means to fans lands better than telling them it is just another match.
